title: Senior's toolkit: the Python debugger
summary: Stop a loop exactly where it goes wrong with breakpoint(), pdb and conditional breakpoints.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: the Python debugger
steps.body: When a loop or a branch does the wrong thing, a debugger beats a page of prints: stop at the right moment, look at every variable, step on. Python ships one, `pdb`, and every editor drives the same idea.

toolkit.what: Pause the program on this line and open the `pdb` prompt. Put it inside an `if` to stop only in the interesting case.
flags: stop only for the case you care about
environment variable that turns every `breakpoint()` off

toolkit.what: Start a script under the debugger. If it crashes, pdb stops at the line that raised (post-mortem), with all the variables still there.
flags: run the script under pdb, paused on the first line
do not pause at the start; run until a breakpoint or a crash

toolkit.what: Moving through code at the `(Pdb)` prompt.
flags: next: run the current line, stepping over calls
step into the function called on this line
run until the current function returns

toolkit.what: Looking around at the `(Pdb)` prompt. You can also type any Python expression.
flags: show the call stack / move up / down a frame

toolkit.what: Set a breakpoint from the prompt, optionally with a condition. `q` quits.
flags: break at line 18 of this file
break there only when the condition is true
quit the debugger and the program

toolkit.what: In the REPL after a crash (for example under `python -i`), open the debugger at the frame that raised.
toolkit.example:
python -i report.py   # it crashes
>>> import pdb; pdb.pm()

toolkit.what: The same debugger in VS Code (Python extension). Right-click the gutter for a conditional breakpoint; tick "Uncaught Exceptions" to stop on crashes.
toolkit.example: Right-click the gutter > Add Conditional Breakpoint > total < 0

steps.prompt: Match each pdb command to what it does.
pairs: run this line, stepping over calls
go into the function called on this line
run on to the next breakpoint
stop debugging and end the program

steps.prompt: A loop over 10,000 orders produces a negative total somewhere around order 7731. Pressing `n` thousands of times is not an option. What do you do?
options: Set a conditional breakpoint, `b 18, order.id == 7731` (or `if order.id == 7731: breakpoint()`), then `c`
Add `print(order)` inside the loop and scroll through 10,000 lines
Run `python -m pdb` and press `s` until you reach it
Delete orders until the bug goes away
steps.explain: A condition makes the debugger stop only when it matters. Even better: break on the symptom itself (`total < 0`), so you do not need to know the order id.

steps.prompt: At the `(Pdb)` prompt, stop at line 18 only once `total` has gone negative.
steps.explain: `b(reak) line, condition` sets a conditional breakpoint. Then `c` runs until it triggers.

steps.prompt: Put this debugging session in order: find why `invoice.py` produces a negative total at line 18.
The nightly CI job has hung for 6 hours. Its last log line is `> /app/report.py(42)build()` followed by `(Pdb)`. What happened, and what is the lasting fix?
options: A `breakpoint()` was committed; remove it, and enable ruff's T100 rule so debugger calls fail the lint
pdb crashed the CI runner; reinstall Python on it
Line 42 has an infinite loop; add a `break`
CI does not support Python; switch the job to a C# runner
steps.explain: `breakpoint()` waits for input that never comes. `PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0` would hide it, but the real fix is to remove it and let the linter (ruff T100, flake8-debugger) catch the next one.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: The moment you add a third debug print, stop and use `breakpoint()` with a condition instead. Run crashing scripts with `python -m pdb -c continue` so you land on the failing line with its variables, and never commit a `breakpoint()`: let the linter guard that.
